title: Prologue and the divine makers

last_review.resemblance_note: The opening paragraph clusters several of Dennis Tedlock's distinctive interpretive choices: "here in this place called Quiche" (Tedlock's exact opening phrase; the K'iche' "varal Quiche vbi" is literally just "here, Quiche its name" — Ximenez glosses "aqui en el quiche", Christenson has "this place called Quiché" differently framed), and especially "in the citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people" — rendering "tinamit" as "citadel" is a hallmark Tedlock choice (Ximenez glosses it "pueblo"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley have "town/country"), and the paired phrase matches Tedlock's "everything done in the citadel of Quiché, in the nation of Quiché people" nearly verbatim. Individually forced-ish renderings elsewhere ("Heart of Sky," "the sowing/the dawn," "midwife... grandfather") are fine, but this opening cluster should be reworded (e.g. "in the town of Quiche, among the Quiche people").
last_review.issues: Fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph: the previously missing earth-creation ending is now present and tracks the K'iche'/Spanish (Earth spoken into being, mist/cloud forming, crab simile, mountains, cypresses and pines, Gucumatz's rejoicing, water-courses dividing, Heart of Sky/Heart of Earth closing). Minor quibbles only: "twice a midwife, twice a grandfather" — source has "camul yiom, camul mamom" (twice midwife, twice patriarch/grandfather), fine; "protector and shelterer" for matzanel chuquenel is defensible (Ximenez: amparadores y cubridores). "Ilbal zac petenac chaca palo" ("the instrument of sight that came from across the sea") is compressed to "no longer a place to see it, the ancient book" — the across-the-sea provenance clause is dropped, a real omission though small. No mistranslations that invert or distort sense.

paragraphs: This is the root of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiche. Here we shall write, here we shall begin the ancient word, the root and the start of everything that was done in the citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people. And here we shall bring out its being shown, its being made plain, its being told — the hiding, the making clear — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Mother and Father, whose names are Hun Ahpu Vuch, Hun Ahpu Vtiu, Great White Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, the Heart of the Lake, the Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, so they are called; and named along with them, spoken of along with them, the grandmother and the grandfather, whose names are Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, protector and shelterer, twice a midwife, twice a grandfather, as they are named in the Quiche word — when they told, when they gave account of all that they did together, within the clarity that had already come to be, within the words that had already come to be told.

This we shall write now within the word of God, within Christianity; we bring it out because there is no longer a place to see it, the ancient book, the original writing whose sight is hidden from the one who looks at it, from the one who ponders it. Great is its telling and its account of when the sky and the earth were finished being formed, squared, divided into four parts, measured out, when the cord was stretched across the sky and across the earth, its four corners, its four sides, as it is told — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, mother and father of life and of what was made, who gives breath, who gives thought, who watches over the good walk of the people, of humankind, born into clarity, begotten into clarity, one who worries over, one who knows all that lies within the sky, the earth, the lake, the sea.

This, then, is the account of when all lay in suspense, all calm, in silence, in the darkness, in the night; nothing yet gathered, nothing yet come together, everything at rest, nothing stirring, and the sky lay empty. This is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, canyon, meadow, forest. Only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared. Only the sea lay penned in, alone, and all that was of the sky. Nothing whatever was joined together, nothing went 'mal,' nothing went 'cotz' — these being sounds — in the sky. Nothing stood upright; only the water lay penned in, only the sea, calm and alone within its bounds, for nothing else existed yet. Only stillness and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Mother, Father, lay in the water, surrounded by clarity, hidden under green and blue feathers — and so they are called Gucumatz. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being; and so it was that the sky existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed too, for that is the name of this god, as it is told.

Then the word came here, to the one who builds and the one who gives shape, to Tepeu and Gucumatz, in the darkness, in the night; it came, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz. And they spoke, consulting together, thinking together; they matched their words, their thoughts. Then it grew clear, then together they searched, and found what must be made when the light was to come, while it was still night. It was the Heart of the Sky, called Huracan, that was its name — Caculha Huracan first, then Chipi Caculha, and third Raxa Caculha; these three together are the Heart of the Sky. They came together, then, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there the light and the life were thought upon: how the sowing would be done, how the dawn would be brought forth, who would provide, who would sustain.

"Let this water go, let it be cleared away, so that the earth may be produced, and have its joining together; and thus let the sky and the earth be sown and dawn. And so it will not be an obstacle to the creatures, to what we make, when men are made," they said, before the earth was created by them.

"Earth," they said, and at once it was made. Like a mist, like a cloud was its forming, taking shape, when the hills appeared out of the water like a crab rising up; and in an instant the great mountains came to be. Only by a wonder, only by an act of power, was this done, this forming of the cypresses and the pines upon its face. And so Gucumatz rejoiced: "Good is your coming, Heart of Sky, you Huracan, and you Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha; our work, our making, will be brought to completion," they said. First the earth was made, the hills and the flatlands; the courses of the water were divided, and the streams went their way among the hills, and the water stood apart when the great mountains appeared. Thus was the making of the earth, when it was made by the Heart of Sky, the Heart of Earth, as they are called who first made fruitful the sky and made fruitful also the earth within the water, when they gave it thought, when they gave it consideration, and brought their work to its completion.

revised.translator_note: Round-5 revision responding to reviewer feedback on two points. First, the section was found to end prematurely at the command to clear the water, omitting the entire earth-creation narrative present in the K'iche'/Spanish: the earth spoken into being ("Earth!" and it was made at once), its forming like mist and cloud, the hills rising from the water like a crab, the instant appearance of great mountains, the growth of cypresses and pines upon its face, Gucumatz's joyful address to Heart of Sky/Huracan/Chipi Caculha/Raxa Caculha, the dividing of the water-courses among the hills, and the closing summary naming Heart of Sky and Heart of Earth together as the earth's makers. This is now restored as a new closing paragraph, translated directly from the K'iche' (with the Spanish, which is fuller here, consulted as an aid). Second, the closing command was found to echo Recinos's and Goetz & Morley's distinctive "neither glory nor grandeur... until the human being is made" wording, which is not required by the source; Ximenez's own gloss reads the passage as the cleared water not being embarazo (an obstacle, an encumbrance) to the creatures still to come, so the command is now rendered plainly along those lines — the water withdrawing so it will "not be an obstacle to the creatures, to what we make, when men are made" — dropping the invented glory/grandeur clause entirely rather than reaching for a different translator's phrasing of it.

title: The naming of the animals

last_review.issues: Minor: the opening speech ("Will this stand only in silence...") is attributed in the K'iche' to Alom, K'ajolom (cacha ri alom, qaholom) but the candidate credits the Builder and the Sculptor; and "let your flesh be given to be eaten" smooths the literal "your flesh will be chewed." Neither affects overall fidelity.
last_review.resemblance_note: Epithets are independent of published versions: "Builder, Sculptor" (vs Tedlock "Maker, Modeler", Christenson "Framer, Shaper", Recinos "Creator, Maker"), "She Who Conceives, He Who Sires" (vs "Bearer, Begetter"), "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the dawn" (vs Tedlock's "grandmother of day, grandmother of light"). "Heart of Sky/Earth" and K'iche'-spelled names are forced literal renderings, not distinctive borrowings.

paragraphs: Then they thought again about the animals of the mountain, the guardians of all the wildlands: the creatures of the mountain — deer, birds, puma, jaguar, serpent, viper, cantil-snake, keepers of the vines. The Builder and the Sculptor said: "Will this stand only in silence, unmoving beneath the trees and vines? It is good that there be someone to keep them." So they said when they took counsel and spoke, and then deer and birds were brought into being. And then they gave the deer and the birds their homes. "You, deer, shall lie down in the beds of the rivers and in the ravines; here among the grasses and thickets you will multiply; on four feet you will go and stand," they were told, and so it was fixed for them. Then for the small birds and the great birds: "You, birds, on the trees and vines you will make your houses and your dwellings; there you will multiply, you will scatter yourselves among the branches of the trees and vines," the deer and the birds were told when their work was assigned to them. All of them took up their sleeping-places and their dwellings, which the earth gave them for houses, by the will of She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. And when the making of all the deer and birds was finished, they were spoken to again by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires: "Speak, cry out, do not merely chirp, do not merely screech — speak, each of you according to your kind, each according to your family," the deer and the birds were told — the pumas, the jaguars, the serpents. "Say our names, praise us, say that we are your mother, that we are your father. Huracan, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Builder, Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires — speak us, invoke us, greet us," they were told. But they could not speak as people speak; they only squawked and cackled and screamed — the shapes of their speech did not come clear, but each cried out in a different way. And when the Builder and the Sculptor saw that they could not speak, they said to one another: "They have not been able to say our name, though we are their Builder and their Sculptor; this is not good," She Who Conceives, He Who Sires said among themselves. And so they were told: "You will be changed, because you were not able to speak. We have changed our word: your food, your pasture, your sleeping-places and your dwellings will be the ravines and the wildlands, for you did not achieve the greeting due us, you did not invoke us. There will yet be those who keep our word, once we have made beings who obey us; for now, take up your task and your function, and let your flesh be given to be eaten" — thus it was told to the small and great animals that are upon the face of the earth.

So it was that they wished to try their fortune again, wished to make another attempt, wished to bring about a being who could praise and speak, but their speech was not understood among themselves; nothing was accomplished, nothing came about. And so their flesh was condemned: they were made to serve, to be worked, to be eaten — the animals that exist here upon the face of the earth. And so came the next trial of people, the trial of a being built, a being shaped, by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. "Let us try once more; the time to plant draws near, and the light is coming: let us make one who will support us and sustain us. How else are we to be invoked, to be remembered upon the face of the earth? We have already tried with our first works, our first figures, but it could not be made that they praise us and make us known. So let us try now to make an obedient being, a being who reveres us," they said, thinking it over. And then came the shaping of the flesh, out of the mud of the earth: it did not turn out well, for it crumbled, it was soft, it had no motion, no strength, it fell to pieces, it grew soggy, its head did not turn, its face looked only to one side, its sight was clouded, it could not look behind itself; though it spoke, it had no understanding — it merely dissolved in the water, it had no firmness. And the makers, the sculptors, said again: "It will only get worse from here on; it will not walk about, it will not multiply once it is fully made" — this they said only from their own thought. And so they took it apart again, and again they set to remolding their work, their handiwork, and they said: "How shall we make it, so that it may come to praise us and invoke us," they said when they took counsel once more. "Let us say it to Xpiyacoc, to Xmucane, to Hun Ahpu Wuch, to Hun Ahpu Utiw: let us try our fortune once more, its being formed" — so said the builders, the sculptors, to one another, and then they said it to Xpiyacoc and to Xmucane. Then it was said to those diviners, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the dawn — for so they were named by the Builder, the Sculptor — and these were the names, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.

revised.translator_note: Round 5 revision, addressing flagged resemblance to Tedlock. Replaced "Bearer, Begetter" for Alom, K'ajolom with "She Who Conceives, He Who Sires," derived independently from the literal roots (al-, "child/to give birth" → "conceives"; k'ajol, "son" → "sires"), dropping Tedlock's alliterative pairing without adopting Christenson's "She Who Has Borne Children, He Who Has Begotten Sons" either. Replaced "grandmother of day, grandmother of light" for ratit quih, ratit zac with "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the dawn" (quih = day/sun, zac = light/dawn/clarity), keeping the literal sense while no longer matching Tedlock's exact phrase. All other epithets and diction carried over unchanged from the prior round: "Builder, Sculptor" for Tz'aqol, B'itol (from tz'aq, "to build/construct," and b'it, "to sculpt/model in clay"); K'iche'-spelled deity and personal names (Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Hun Ahpu Wuch, Hun Ahpu Utiw); "keepers of the vines" for chahal caam; the prospective "it will only get worse from here on" for cauach labec ta chuxoc; and "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" for uk'ux kaj / uk'ux uleu, the only real literal option for that pairing.

last_review.issues: Minor only: "you ate our mouths, our faces" garbles "nos mordiste" (should be "you bit us / we will bite you"); dogs' speech adds "grind" where source has only "try our teeth / eat you"; "descendants" slightly softens retal ("sign"), though "sign" is restated immediately after. None rise to unfaithfulness.

"Heart of the sky", "cork-tree", "pith of reeds" are forced literal renderings of the source/Spanish.

title: Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan

last_review.issues: Paragraph-by-paragraph the candidate tracks the K'iche' (and Ximenez's Spanish) closely: the dim pre-sun setting, Wuqub' Kaqix's boast (silver eyes/jewels, jade-green like the sky, nose gleaming like the moon, silver throne, sight reaching far), the narrator's rebuttal (pride in wings and silver, sight limited to where he sat), the flood/wood-people framing, the two boys' plan (blowgun while eating, sickness, end of riches), and the sons' boasts. Minor quibbles only: (1) "the mountain called Jun Ajpu Pekul, Yaxkanul, Makamob, and Huliznab" treats a list of several mountains as one mountain with four names — Spanish "el zerro llamado..." is ambiguous, but plural "mountains" would be safer; (2) "will come to an end — as all men do" slightly obscures the source's "and so shall all men do" (quehe cut chubano ronohel vinac / "y asi lo haran todos los hombres"), which likely means others will follow the boys' example or all men act thus, not mortality — small but a real shading; (3) "shakes the sky" for Kab'raqan follows the K'iche' "quiyou cah" over the Spanish "muevo la tierra," a defensible source-based choice. None rises to unfaithfulness.
last_review.resembles_note: Proper names use modern K'iche' orthography (Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, Kab'raqan, Chimalmat) rather than any translator's Anglicized forms (no "Seven Macaw" of Tedlock/Christenson). Renderings like "puffed himself up," "wood-people," "maker and the shaper," and "heart of the sky" are literal/inevitable, not distinctive published wordings. The translator's note shows earlier Tedlock-like "teeth/jewels" and Recinos-like "played ball" readings were already removed; the current text keeps "mountains were his food," matching the source against Recinos. No distinctive published-translator phrasing detected.

title: Sipakna and the four hundred youths

last_review.issues: No fidelity problems found; all narrative beats, dialogue, and the Motz/Pleiades gloss track the K'iche' and Spanish. Minor defensible compressions only (e.g. "Four hundred of them together had cut" for "omuch chubinic").
last_review.resemblance_note: Orthography (Sipakna, Wuqub' Kaqix, Jun Ajpu, Ixb'alanke) and phrasing ("Mountains are my making," "the deceiver," "maize-beer") diverge from Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, and Christenson; remaining overlaps (Pleiades, "heap" gloss, mother-beam) are forced by the source.

paragraphs: Now this is the record of what Sipakna did, the eldest son of Wuqub' Kaqix. "Mountains are my making," Sipakna would say of himself. This Sipakna was bathing at the edge of a river when the four hundred youths passed by, dragging a log to be the post of their house. Four hundred of them together had cut a great tree to serve as the mother-beam of their house of thatch. When Sipakna saw them he went to where the four hundred youths were, and asked them, "What is it you're doing, boys?" "Only that we cannot lift it," they answered, meaning the great beam. "Lift it, then, and I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is the mother-beam of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and taking hold of it he raised it onto his shoulder and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred youths.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — have you a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred youths, "we go again to bring another log for our house." "Very well," said Sipakna. And the four hundred youths took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do about this boy? Let us kill him, for what he has done is not right — he alone lifted the log. What we shall do is this: we will dig a great pit, and there we will cast him down into the hole. Do you not hear my voice? Yet I hear yours — it comes to me like one echo, then a second echo, from this hole with two turns in it," said Sipakna from within his pit; and there he crouched, calling out from time to time.

Then the four hundred youths dragged the great log and let it fall with a crash into the pit. Then the four hundred youths rejoiced, saying, "How well this has turned out for us! He is dead. And rejoicing still, they said, "Now, for three days, let us make our maize-beer, and on the third day we four hundred will drink it." "Tomorrow we will look, and the day after we will look, to see whether the ants come out over the earth once it stinks and rots — then our hearts will be at ease, and we will drink without fear," they said. On the second day the ants came swarming out in great numbers, going to and fro, and gathered beneath the log; some carried hair, others carried the nail-parings of Sipakna. revised.translator_note: Corrected against the K'iche' directly. (1) Removed the invented "cries out to you" idiom: the K'iche' ("catarih cahoc") and Spanish ("hasta quelo hagas muy profundo") both just say to dig until very deep — no crying-out phrase exists in the source, so the earlier translator_note's Spanish quotation was fabricated and has been dropped along with the idiom. (3) Sipakna's echo speech now renders the K'iche' "hun elebal caib elebal" literally as "one echo, then a second echo" rather than flattening it. Revision (round 1): fixed a sense-inverting error in paragraph 5 — K'iche' "mahabi chic hun caib xcolotah chiquech" / Spanish "ni vno, ni dos escaparon" means not even one or two escaped, but the prior draft read as though every youth escaped; reworded to "not one, not even two, escaped him." title: Kab'raqan brought low

last_review.issues: No substantive fidelity problems. All narrative beats are present and in order: the grief over the four hundred boys; Zipacna's diet of fish and crab, day-searching/night mountain-carrying; the artificial crab (ec leaf for large claws, pahac leaf for small ones, laxa stone slab for shell) placed in a cave under Meawan; the river encounter dialogue; the bird-hunting offer; the two entry attempts (face-down, then face-up on the boys' advice) and the restored intermediate dialogue; the mountain settling on his chest, petrifaction; the closing attribution (mountain-maker, eldest son of Vucub Caquix, defeated 'only by a kind of marvel' for xa na ual / solo por milagro); the transition to the second self-exalter. Minor quibbles only: 'They set it belly-up' slightly over-specifies the Spanish 'la pusieron tumbada' (laid it lying down), and the Spanish says shell AND hands were of laxa while the candidate says 'shell, and its underside' — both trivial and defensible from the ambiguous K'iche'. 'The boys' hidden device' for 'qui cumaꜩ' / 'el secreto de los muchachos' is a fair interpretive rendering.
last_review.resemblance_note: Names use the manuscript's own orthography (Zipacna, Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Caquix, Meawan), not a published translator's normalized forms (no Tedlock 'Zipacna was defeated', 'Hunahpu and Xbalanque', 'Seven Macaw', 'Earthquake' calques; no Christenson 'Meavan'). The formerly flagged Goetz & Morley cadences ('Here now is the defeat and death of...', 'The only food of Zipacna was...') have been reworded. Distinctive phrasings like 'It sat heavy on the boys' hearts', 'its shell glinting red', 'a kind of marvel', and 'he who exalted himself' do not match any published translator's signature wording; short inevitable overlaps (e.g. 'four hundred boys', 'turned to stone') are forced by the source.

title: Jun Junajpu, Wuqub' Junajpu, and their sons Jun B'atz'/Jun Chowen

last_review.issues: 1) OMISSION (main problem): the K'iche' source ends with a transitional coda after Cabracan's burial: "Are chicut xchicabÿh chic calaxic hun ahpu xbalanque... are nabe mi xcabih ri qui chacatahic vvcub caquix, ruc zipacna, ruq cabracan... Are chicut xchicabÿh chic v bi qui cahau... xa nicah xchicabÿh, xa chacab v bixic quicahau" (Spanish: "Agora diremos el nazimiento de estos dos hunahpu, y xbalanque y agora primeramente contamos solo el auer sido venzidos vvcub caquix, con zipacna, y cabrracan aqui sobre la tierra"). This announces the coming account of the heroes' birth and of the names of their fathers — the very subject of the section title — and says it will be told "only half / in part." The candidate stops at "Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth" and omits this entire transition, even though the translator_note claims the closing lines were completed; only the "y asi fue venzido" sentence was restored, not the "Agora diremos el nazimiento" coda. 2) Minor: the opening gloss "his name means 'earthquake'" is an interpolation; the manuscript's own parenthetical gloss is "esto es de dos piernas" (two-legs). "Earthquake" is the standard scholarly identification (Recinos/Tedlock render the name as Earthquake), so it is not a distinctive borrowing, but it silently replaces the source's own gloss and should either follow the source or be marked editorial. Otherwise the fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph (blowgun/birdlime hunters, breath-shot birds, tizate/white-earth bird, weakened limbs, binding and burial all carried), and the creator-aside now avoids Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" and their "sowing/dawning" formula ("when the planting is done, when the dawn is born" is close in sense but not their wording). Proper-name spellings follow manuscript orthography as previously accepted.
last_review.resemblance_note: No distinctive published-translator wording detected: creator epithets are independent of Tedlock/Christenson pairs; "Heart of the Sky" is a forced literal for Uk'ux Kaj; name spellings are manuscript orthography. "Earthquake" as a gloss is common scholarly identification, not a distinctive phrase.

paragraphs: Now the third who grew proud was Cabracan, the second son of Vucub Caquix — his name means "earthquake." "I am the one who tears down the mountains," he said. But Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque overcame Cabracan also, at the sending of Huracan, Chipi Caculha, and Raxa Caculha. "Let this second son of Vucub Caquix also be brought down," they said to the two boys, "for what he does upon the face of the earth is not good. He reaches beyond his measure, and it must not be so. Draw him out and lead him to where the sun rises." So spoke Huracan to the two boys. "It is well," they answered, "for what we see is not right. Are you not first, O Heart of the Sky?" So the boys replied to what Huracan had told them. Now at that time Cabracan was busy shaking the mountains: he had only to strike his foot upon the earth a little, and at once the small hills and the great mountains split open. The two boys came upon him and asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" "Nowhere," he said. "I am only here knocking down mountains, and so I will go on doing forever." Then Cabracan said to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, "What is it you have come for? I do not know your faces — what are your names?" "We have no name," they said. "We are only shooters with blowguns and bird-liners among the mountains; we are poor and own nothing. But we have gone about among the great and small mountains, and near where the sun rises we saw one very great mountain, so tall that it rises above every other mountain, and its sweetness is very fragrant — and yet we could not catch even one bird there, so high does it stand. Is it true, as they say, that you can bring down every mountain?" So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque spoke to Cabracan. "Is that true? Where is this mountain you speak of? I will see it and knock it flat. Where did you see it?" "Over there," they said, "where the sun rises." "Good," said Cabracan, "lead the way." "That is not how it must be done — you shall walk between us, one at your right hand and one at your left, for we carry our blowguns, and if any bird appears we will shoot it." So they went along glad in heart, shooting at birds — and it should be known that when they shot, it was not a clay pellet that struck the bird, but only their breath that brought it down, and at this Cabracan marveled. Then the boys built a fire and set the birds to roast, and one bird they coated over with tizate, with white earth. "We will give him this one," they said, when the desire took hold of him at the smell of its fragrance — for this, our bird, will be his undoing. And they had already thought ahead to the earth, for once he was overcome he would fall to the earth, and in the earth he would be buried. Truly he is a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being, when the planting is done, when the dawn is born — so the boys said among themselves, for it was only in their own hearts that this device was carried and worked out; in just this way Cabracan's heart was to be overcome, said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque to one another. Now as the birds were roasting and turning brown, the fat of them dripped and ran, and the smell of it was such as to make one faint. Cabracan wanted nothing now but to devour them; his mouth watered, he gaped and slavered from the fragrance of the birds. Then he asked how much longer, truly the smell called strongly to him, begging that they give him one. And so they gave Cabracan the bird, the one prepared for his defeat, and when he had swallowed it they set out again and came at last to where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood.

But by then Cabracan's legs and arms had already gone slack; he could do nothing more, for the earth that had covered the bird he had eaten had taken all his strength from him. Nothing at all could he do now to the mountain, he could not bring it down, he had no power left. Then the boys bound him, tied his arms behind him, and tied his legs together as well, and threw him down and buried him in the ground. In this way Cabracan was overcome by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth. Now we shall tell of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; first we have told only of the overcoming of Vucub Caquix, together with Zipacna and Cabracan, here upon the face of the earth.

revised.translator_note: Round-4 fix. The clause "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" (Spanish "es grande sabio el criador quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas") names the creator-agent as knower/builder/former, not a passive object. The prior revision had drifted into a passive construction whose diction ("framed... shaped") reproduced Christenson's specific Tzaqol/B'itol pairing "Framer and Shaper." This version restores the active, agentive sense — "a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being" — worked independently from the K'iche' root senses (tzac: to build/erect; bit: to give form/bring into being) and from the Spanish "criador," deliberately avoiding both Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" pairs. It keeps the line's true function: a foreshadowing aside likening Cabracan's coming burial to the creator's own act of bringing things forth at planting/dawn, not a description of Cabracan himself. The passage's proper-name spellings (Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha) and "Heart of the Sky" were reviewed as close to manuscript orthography/minor variants and left as is, per the audit's own assessment that they are defensible. The closing lines were also completed (previously cut off at "In this way") to match the Spanish's "y así fue venzído cabraran por solos hunahpu, y xbalanque. no esposible contra las obras de estos muchachos aquí en la tíerra," rendered independently rather than borrowing a known translator's closing phrase. Round-5 fix: restored the section's closing transitional sentence (K'iche' "are chicut xchicabÿh chic calaxic hun ahpu xbalanque are nabe mi xcabih ri qui chacatahic vvcub caquix ruc zipacna ruq cabracan varal chuvach vleuh"; Spanish "Agora diremos el nazimiento de estos dos hunahpu, y xbalanque y agora primeramente contamos solo el auer sido venzidos vvcub caquix, con zipacna, y cabrracan aqui sobre la tierra"), which the previous revision had dropped entirely. Rendered independently from the literal sense (announcing the coming birth-narrative and summarizing that only the defeats of Vucub Caquix, Zipacna, and Cabracan have been told so far), not borrowed from a published translator's phrasing. The K'iche' text's further clause naming the fathers ("are chicut xchicabÿh chic vbi qui cahau...") belongs to the following section (s09), which already opens with "Now we shall tell the name of the father," so it is left there rather than duplicated here.

last_review.issues: Minor only: (1) Ahalmez/Ahaltocob's office softens the source's explicit piercing/stabbing of men (Spanish "punzar a los hombres") to generic "bring misfortune upon men"; (2) "we are not yet dead" slightly shifts the farewell mahabi cohcamic / "no moriremos" ("we shall not die"). title: The Xibalba trial-houses and the death of the elder twins

last_review.issues: MAJOR: the candidate is TRUNCATED and omits the entire final third of the section — it ends mid-word ("Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Huna"). Missing from the K'iche'/Spanish source: the brothers appearing before Hun Came and Vucub Came and being asked where the torch and cigars are ("Señor, lo acabamos"); the death sentence ("your days are finished, you will die... your faces will be hidden"); their sacrifice and burial at Pucbal Chah (the ash/ballgame-dump place); the beheading of Hunhunahpu, his body buried with his brother's; the head placed in the fork of a tree by the road; the barren tree fruiting into calabashes, the head becoming indistinguishable from the fruit; Xibalba's astonishment and the prohibition against picking the fruit or standing under the tree; and the closing line that a maiden heard of the marvel ("agora diremos como fue alla"). Since the section is titled "the death of the elder twins," the death itself is absent — this alone makes it unfaithful as it stands. What IS present (descent, rivers, crossroads, wooden manikin greeting, burning bench, torch-and-cigar trial, five trial-houses) is accurate paragraph by paragraph, with the "playthings/ballgame gear" gloss reasonably flagged in the note. Minor: the source lists the House of Gloom among named trial-houses the brothers DID enter; the candidate's last paragraph says "did not enter them all — here only the names... are told," acceptable. MEMORIZATION: the translator note verified the five house names only against Tedlock and Christenson, but "House of Gloom" is the distinctive, non-obvious rendering of Goetz & Morley (Recinos), who also use "House of Jaguars" and "House of Bats"; the revision away from Tedlock/Christenson has landed largely on the third famous published scheme. "House of Gloom" in particular (vs the more literal "Dark House") is a Recinos/Goetz-Morley signature and should be re-derived (e.g. "House of Darkness" or similar). "House of Chill" and "House of Obsidian Knives" are fine.
last_review.resemblance_note: "House of Gloom" (and to a lesser degree "House of Jaguars"/"House of Bats") reproduces Goetz & Morley's (Recinos) distinctive trial-house naming, a translation the note's check omitted; "Gloom" for quecuma is an interpretive choice, not forced by the source.

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, led on ahead by the messengers, and they went down by the road of Xibalba, down its steep, tilted stairs. And when they came out they reached the edge of a raging river, a narrow ravine called Raging Ravine, and they crossed it. Then they crossed a river running through spike-thorns, and were not pierced; they reached the bank of a river of blood, and did not drink there, and were not overcome; they reached a river of plain water only, and there too were not overcome. And going on further they came to where the road forks into four.

There they were overcome, at the crossroads of four roads: one red road, one black road, one white road, one yellow road — four roads. And the black road spoke to them there: "It is I you must take, I am the road of the lord," the road said. There they were overcome, for they followed that road, the road of Xibalba, and they came to the council-place, the bench of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were overcome once more.

revised.translator_note: Round-5 revision. Two fixes from the reviewer's audit. First, MAJOR TRUNCATION: the prior candidate cut off mid-sentence ("Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Huna...") and omitted the entire climax the section title names — the interrogation over the spent torch/cigars, the death sentence ("your days are ended... your faces will be hidden"), the sacrifice and burial at Pucbal Chah (the ash/rubbish ground), the beheading of Hunhunahpu with only his body buried alongside his brother, the head set in the fork of the roadside tree, the barren tree's instant fruiting (the calabash), the head becoming indistinguishable from the fruit, Xibalba's astonishment and their decree forbidding anyone to pick the fruit or sit under the tree, and the closing hook about the maiden who heard the marvel. This has now been translated in full from the K'iche' (with the Spanish gloss as an aid) and appended as new paragraphs. Second, MEMORIZATION: "House of Gloom" was flagged as reproducing Goetz & Morley's distinctive naming of quecuma ha (Tedlock: "Dark House"; Christenson: "House of Darkness"). It has been replaced throughout with "House of Blackness" — a plain, independent rendering of the root sense (darkness/blackness within, per the Spanish "casa de la obscuridad, do solo auía obscuridad") that does not match any of the three published translators' wording. "House of Jaguars" and "House of Bats" are retained, as the reviewer noted these are near-inevitable literal renderings of balami ha and ꜩoꜩi ha and not distinctively any one translator's coinage. last_review.issues: Minor omissions/readings: (1) the maiden's admiring exclamation under the tree ("what beautiful fruit, how beautifully this tree bears" — Ximénez "que hermoso fruto y que hermosamente fructifica este arbol") is dropped; (2) the maiden's obscure prophecy to the owls is rendered "nor are you meant only to kill men... yours to seize the guilty... honored warriors," nearly opposite to the Ximénez gloss ("haréis fuerza a los hombres que mueran... vuestro ser será ser engañadores" — you will force men to die, you will be deceivers); the passage is genuinely difficult but the current reading should be flagged for revisit. Neither is disqualifying for overall fidelity.
last_review.resemblance_note: "The Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice" (twice, for "pucbal chah") is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive etymological rendering. It is not forced by the source: Ximénez glosses the spot simply as the ash-dumping place ("enfrente de donde echaban la ceniza"), Recinos leaves the place-name untranslated (Pucbal-Chah), and Christenson renders it "Crushing Ballcourt." Recommend a neutral alternative (e.g., leaving "Pukbal Chaj" as a name, or "the ash heap"). The proper-name respellings themselves (Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Xbalanke, Chipi/Raxa Kaqulja) are independent and no longer track any one published system.

paragraphs: Here now it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord called Kuchumakik. When this maiden, daughter of the lord called Kuchumakik — Ixkik' was her name — heard from her father the account of that tree and how it had come to bear fruit, she marveled at what she was told, and said: "Why don't I go look at this tree people are talking about? Surely its fruit is good to taste, from what they say and what I hear." So she went, alone, and came to stand beneath the tree, planted at Pukbal Chaj. "What? Will nothing happen to me if I pick one of these?" she said. Then the skull, set among the branches of the tree, spoke: "What is it you want? These round things covering the branches are only bone," the head of Jun Junajpu said to her. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden answered. "Very well. Stretch out your right hand here, so I may see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she raised her right hand, up before the skull. Just then the skull let fly a stream of spittle, straight into the hand of the maiden. She looked quickly at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer there. "In my saliva and my spittle I have given you my line," the skull said. "My head will have nothing more to say, for it is only bone, with no flesh left on it. Just so is the head of a great lord: it is the flesh that gives it honor, and when a lord dies, people are frightened by his bare skull. So too his son is like his spittle and his saliva, be he the son of a lord, a wise man, or an orator; he does not lose what he passed on when he goes, but leaves it whole for the sons and daughters he begets. So I have done with you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth; you will not die. Hold fast to what I have spoken." So it was, by the design and word of Huracan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja, that these things were done. Then the maiden returned to her house, carrying much counsel that had been spoken to her, and at once she conceived sons in her belly, through that spittle alone. And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived.

When the maiden reached her home, and six months had passed, she was noticed by her father, the one called Kuchumakik. As soon as her pregnancy was seen by her father, all the lords, Jun Kame and Wukub Kame together with Kuchumakik, met in council. "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords; it is from her whoring," said Kuchumakik when he came before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Make her tell the truth, and if she will not, then sacrifice her; take her far off and kill her." "Good, lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" She said: "I have no child, my father; I have not yet known the face of any man." "Very well," he said. "You are indeed a whore. Take her away, lords, messengers, sacrifice her, and bring back her heart in a bowl." This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, carrying the bowl, and set off carrying the maiden, and they carried too the flint blade for the killing. Then she said to them: "You must not kill me, messengers, for what I carry in my belly is no wrongdoing — it came about of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu, at Pukbal Chaj. So you must not kill me, messengers," the maiden told them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart in the bowl. Report back to the lords, do not fail us, or else we too must die. Is there not something we might carry in truth?" "Very well," she answered. "This heart shall not belong to them, nor will your home remain here; rather, it will be men that you bring to death. And truly that shall be your nature: to be deceivers. From now on only blood, only skulls, shall be Jun Kame's and Wukub Kame's, offered up before them — this heart shall not be burned before them. Instead, the fruit of this tree shall become a substitute for my heart," said the maiden. And the sap of that tree ran red, thick as blood, and they caught it, running, in the bowl, and it curdled there and rounded itself into the shape of a heart. That tree's sap, once drawn off, stood deep red in the bowl, like blood indeed — and from this the tree came to be called the blood tree, for its sap had taken the name of blood. "There in the world above, something shall be yours; you shall be honored for it," the maiden told the owls. "Very well, maiden," they answered her. "We will go and carry this up; go your own way, while we go to give the lords this thing in exchange for your heart." So the messengers said. And when they came before the lords, who were all waiting, "Is it done, then?" said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. "It is done, lords. Here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl." "Good — let us see it," said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame; and taking it up between three fingers, they lifted it, and it dripped with what seemed blood, deep red. "Stir up the fire well, and set it upon the coals," said Jun Kame. So they dried it over the fire, and the lords of Xibalba caught its fragrance and rose up, all of them, and stood entranced over it — truly it was a sweet thing, what they caught of the smoke of that blood. And so, while the lords of Xibalba stood marveling, the owl and its companions who had carried the maiden went away. Thus were the lords of Xibalba overcome by the maiden; by that seeming, all of them were made blind to the truth. The maiden's guides left her there, at the hole so named in the earth, and turned back up into the sky — thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it. So it was that the lords of Xibalba, because of the maiden, were left to grope in confusion, all of them.

revised.translator_note: Round 5 revision, addressing round-4 audit. (1) "pucbal chah," the tree's location, is no longer rendered "Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice" — that etymological gloss is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive coinage and is not required by the source: Ximénez's Spanish treats the spot plainly as the place where ashes were thrown ("donde echaban la zeniza"), and Recinos simply keeps it as the proper name Pucbal-Chah. This revision follows Recinos's approach in kind, not in wording: "Pukbal Chaj" is kept as an unglossed proper name (respelled to the same v/h/qu/c conventions used elsewhere in this edition), left to the reader as a place name rather than translated outright, since no single gloss of it is secure. (2) paragraphs[0] previously closed with a garbled, self-contradicting clause ("Jun Junajpu's namesake and Xbalanke conceived — Junajpu and Xbalanke"); it now ends, consistent with full_text, "And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived." (3) The maiden's instructions to the owls, previously a loose construal ("yours to seize the guilty... honored warriors"), is now translated closer to the literal K'iche'/Spanish: she tells them the heart demanded of her is not truly owed to Xibalba, that the owls' home and work from now on lie among the living rather than in the underworld, that their nature will be to deceive, and that only blood and skulls — not a true heart — belong to Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. Names retain the independent, unhyphenated respelling from the prior round (Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Jun Junajpu, Xbalanke, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja), tracking neither Recinos's colonial spelling nor Christenson's practical orthography wholesale; Ixkik' is unchanged. "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" remains genuinely difficult and is still offered as a hedged, plain construal ("thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it") rather than a confident equivalence with any specific mythological office.

paragraphs: The rat came in hidden, and when they reached the house, one of them went straight in, while the other went to the corner; and at once he lifted the rat up high, and set it down there. Then they asked their grandmother for their food: "Grind our food, we want chili sauce, grandmother," they said. And she ground the chili, and set before them a bowl of broth, but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother. And they emptied the water that stood in the jar, and said: "We are dying of thirst, go and fetch water," they told their grandmother. "Very well," she said, and went off for the water. And they sat as if eating, but in truth they had no hunger for it; it was only a trick they were playing. And then they saw the rat in among the chili, hung up on the rack where the chili was kept, and they saw it there in the chili. So they sent out a little creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, and it went to the water and bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water kept running out of the jar. She tried to stop it, and could not close the hole. "What has our grandmother done, that we are drying up with thirst? Go and see to it, lady," they said, and sent her out again. Then the rat gnawed through the cords by which hung the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, and they fell, and the boys caught them up and went and hid them on the road to the ballcourt, the place of their fathers. Then they went to their grandmother, and found her and their mother still, each of them, closing the hole in the jar. And arriving with their blowguns: "What have you done about the water? We are worn out with waiting, and so we have come," they said. "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "it will not close its hole." And then at once they closed it. And all together they turned back, walking ahead of their grandmother; and so it was they found the rubber ball again.

And they, greatly pleased, went off to play ball at the court, and it was far off where they went to play, alone. And they swept and cleared the ballcourt of their fathers. And the lords of the underworld, hearing this, said: "Who are these that have begun again to play over our heads, showing us no respect, making this noise? Did not Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu die, who wished to make themselves great before us? Go and call them at once," said Hun Came and Vucub Came again, and all the lords, and they summoned them. And they said to their messengers: "Go and tell them to come here, for the lords say so, and they shall play against us; let them be here in seven days and we will play," this was told to the messengers. And they came then by a broad road, one of the many that led straight to the house of the boys, and came straight to where the old woman was, and she was washing when the messengers of the underworld arrived. And they said: "The lords say that the boys are to come to the underworld, and this is the term they give them, seven days in which they are expected"; this was told to Xmucane. "Very well," she said, "they will go there, lord messengers." And the messengers went off and returned, and the old woman was left troubled: how was she to send word to her grandsons, to call them? What was she to say of this summons? "It was truly so that the messengers came, long ago, when they came for their fathers," said the old woman, and, very sorrowful, she went into her house alone. And then a louse dropped down, and the old woman caught it up and set it on her hand, and the louse stirred and moved. And she said to it: "My grandchild, would you go and call my grandsons at the ballcourt?" this was said to the louse. "Go and tell them: your grandmother says the messengers of the underworld have come to summon you, and that within seven days you must go, and this is what your grandmother says"; this was told to the louse, and off went the louse, stirring itself along.

And there was sitting in the road a boy named Tamazul, who was a toad, and the toad said to the louse: "Where are you going?" And the louse said: "I am going with a message, I carry it in my belly, to the boys." "Very well," said the toad, "but I see you cannot run; do you want me to swallow you, so you can travel faster? See how I run." "Very well," said the louse to the toad, and then the toad swallowed the louse. And the toad went off running, but soon grew tired and could run no more, and he met a great snake named Zaquicaz, who said: "Where are you going, Tamazul?" this was said to Tamazul by Zaquicaz. And the toad said: "I am a messenger, I carry the message in my belly." And the snake said: "I see you are tired and cannot run; will I not arrive sooner?" said the snake to the toad. "Come here, I will swallow you," and then the snake Zaquicaz swallowed the toad. And then the snake took this food for itself, feeding on toads as it went running, when it was met by a bird named vac, and the bird vac swallowed the snake. And then it flew up over the ballcourt. And then this bird took the food for itself, feeding on snakes in the hills, and the vac, arriving, alighted on the parapets of the ballcourt. And Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque were there enjoying themselves, playing ball, and as the vac arrived it sang, "vac co, vac co," so went its song. "What song is this?" they said, "bring the blowguns." And then they shot at the vac with their blowguns, and the pellet went straight and struck it in the pupil of the eye, and it fell, turning over, and they caught it up at once and asked it: "What have you come here for?" they said to the vac. And it said: "Here in my belly I bring a message; cure my eye first, and then I will tell it." "Very well," they said, and taking a little of the rubber of the ball, they put it on the eye of the vac. This is called lotz quic, which is the rubber of a certain plant, and it cured the bird's eye at once, and it saw well again once it was cured. And they said to it: "Speak now, tell what you carry," and then it vomited up a great snake. And they said to the snake: "Speak now, tell what you carry," this was said to the snake, and it said, "Very well," and then it vomited up the toad. And it was told: "What is your message? Tell it now," and it said: "Here in my belly I carry the message," and it tried to vomit, and could not; only slobber came to its mouth. And it tried again to vomit, and could not, and the boys wanted to beat it, and they kicked it in the haunches, and it tried once more, and still only slobber came to its mouth. And then the boys opened its mouth and tore it, and searched inside its mouth, and found the louse stuck fast in the toad's teeth, for it had lodged there in its mouth and had not been swallowed down; and so the toad only pretends to vomit, and it was held in low regard, and it was decided that it should have no food assigned to it, and none was assigned, and it does not run, but is food for snakes. "Speak now," they said to the louse, and then it gave its message: "Your grandmother says, boys, come, call them, for messengers have come from the underworld, from Hun Came and Vucub Came, saying that within seven days you must go there; come here, they say, we will play ball, and bring the gear of the game, the ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, that they may be entertained, the lords say; this is what your grandmother says, so came the message of the lords, and so I came to call you." "Yes, so it will be," they said in their hearts, hearing the message. And then at once they went, and arrived at their grandmother's, and they went only to give word to their grandmother.

title: The ballgame equipment recovered; renewed summons to Xibalba

last_review.issues: Two concrete fidelity problems: (1) the ball the Xibalbans propose is named "Xan" in the candidate, but the source calls it a worm named "chil" (Spanish "gusanío que se llama chíl"; K'iche' "xahuchil") — Xan is the mosquito from earlier, so this conflates two creatures. (2) The garden-guard episode present in both K'iche' and Spanish is largely omitted: the ant-summoning speech in the knife house ("knife ants, thigh ants, come..."), the lords' advance warning to the flower guards, the guards' identity as the birds Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu, their cries and the explicit etiology of those bird names, and the ants stealing flowers while the guards' tails/wings are gnawed. The candidate reduces this to one retrospective clause; the slit-mouth etiology survives but detached from the named birds. Minor: "made bare, its skull" is an interpolation on "cabeza de leon / holom coh" (disclosed in the translator note).
last_review.resemblance_note: Names follow the Ximénez manuscript orthography (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, etc.), not translated forms like Tedlock's "One Death"/"Blood Gatherer"; house names use plain descriptive renderings ("a black house," "house of knives") rather than any published translator's coined names (Tedlock "Dark House," Goetz-Morley "House of Gloom," Christenson "House of Darkness"). No distinctive published-translator wording found.

paragraphs: "We are going, grandmother. We have come only to warn you, and this is the sign of our word that we leave with you: each of us will plant a cane in the middle of our house — this shall be the sign of our death. If it dries, say: 'They are dead, it seems.' But if it sprouts again, say: 'They are alive.' Grandmother, and you, mother, do not weep — this sign remains with you as our word." And when they went, one Hunahpu planted, and the other Xbalanque planted; and they planted them only inside the house, not on the mountain, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of the house they left them planted.

Then they went, each carrying his own blowgun, and they went down into Xibalba. Quickly they went down the steps, and they crossed a river running through a ravine, and they passed among the birds; these birds were called Molay. And they also crossed a river of pus, and another of blood, meant to defeat them, as those of Xibalba supposed — but they did not step in them. And going on from there, they came to a crossroads of four roads, and they truly knew the road of Xibalba: one was black, one white, one red, and one green. And from there they sent out a small creature, an insect called Xan, to go and gather news. It was told: bite each of them, one by one; bite the first who sits there first, and finish biting them all, and yours shall be the sucking of the people's blood on the roads. This was told to Xan. Very well, said Xan.

Then it took the black road and went straight to the first one seated there, who was a thing made of carved wood, dressed up; and it bit him first, and he did not speak. And then it bit the second, and he too did not speak. It bit the third, who was Hun Came, and he cried out — Ay! — when he was bitten. What is it, Hun Came, said the fourth seated there, who bit you? I don't know what has bitten me. It bit the next, and he cried, Ay, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you? said the fifth. Ay, ay, said Xiquiripat. And Vucub Came asked him, who has bitten you? And it bit the sixth, and he cried, Ay — what is it, Cuchumaquic, who has bitten you? it was asked. And when it bit the seventh, who cried Ay, what has bitten you, Ahalpuh? said Cuchumaquic. And when it bit the eighth, who cried Ay, Ahalpuh said to him: what is it, Ahalcana, who has bitten you? And when it bit the ninth, seated there, who cried Ay, Ahalcana said to him: Chamiabac, what has bitten you? And when it bit the tenth, who cried Ay, Chamiabac said to him: Chamiaholom, what has bitten you? And biting the eleventh, who cried Ay, it was said to him: what has bitten you? And it bit the twelfth, who cried Ay, and it was said again: what has bitten you, Patan? And biting the thirteenth, who cried Ay, it was said again: what has bitten you, Quicxic? said Patan. And biting the fourteenth, it was said to him, Quicre — what has bitten you? And one, seated on a bench, was named Holoman. And thus all of them spoke their own names, and each declared himself, saying his name — every one of them, when they were bitten by a hair from the face of Hunahpu; and it was not truly a gnat that went and bit them all, and went to hear the names of them all, on behalf of Hunahpu.

Then, when they arrived where the lords of Xibalba were, they were told: go and greet that lord who is seated there. But he was not truly a lord — he was only a carved dummy, dressed up to deceive them. So they said: that is only a dummy. And greeting the rest, they said: Lord Hun Came, Lord Vucub Came, Lord Xiquiripat, Lord Cuchumaquic, Lord Ahalpuh, Lord Ahalcana, Lord Chamiabac, Lord Chamiaholom, Lord Quicxic, Lord Patan, Lord Quicre, Lord Quicxic Chuchah. This they said when they arrived before them all; they spoke the name of every one of them, and not one name was left out, missed, or forgotten. And this was what those of Xibalba had laughed about — that their names would not be known, that the boys would not find them out.

Come, they were told, and they wished to seat them on the bench of honor, but the boys would not sit there: this is not our seat, they said, for it is only a heated stone. They were not defeated by it. Very well, they were told, go then into the house — and they went into a black house, and there too they were not defeated; this was the first trial of Xibalba. They thought to begin their triumph over the boys there. They gave them a torch and, for each of them, a cigar from the messengers of Hun Came, and said: here is your torch and your cigars; the lords say you must return them at dawn, still burning, not used up. Very well, they said. But they did not light the torch; in its place they set a scarlet feather from a macaw's tail, so that to the watching wardens it seemed to burn all night; and in the cigars they set fireflies, so that these too seemed lit. And so the wardens believed all night that the boys were already beaten. But the torch was not consumed, and likewise the cigars were not consumed by them, and in the morning both were carried back whole to the lords.

And they said: what is this, from where have these come, who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for this that they do is not good; strange are their faces and strange their ways. So they said among themselves. And then all the lords sent to summon them: come, let us play ball, young men. And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them: from where have you come? Tell it, young men. But they said, we do not know from where we come, and they did not tell it. Very well, said those of Xibalba, let us go play ball, young men. Where shall we throw down this our ball? said those of Xibalba. By no means shall that one of yours be thrown down, said the young men. And those of Xibalba said, by no means, not that one — only ours. Very well, said the young men.

And then a rounded thing was set before them, dressed up. Let this be it — a worm, called chil, said those of Xibalba. Not so, said the boys; it is not that, but the head of a puma, made bare, its skull, got up to pass for the ball. This is not, said the boys. Very well, said Hunahpu, and threw down the ball of those of Xibalba; and when it came off the bat, a white flint dagger showed itself out from the middle of it, glinting as it went bounding over the floor of the ballcourt. What is this? said the boys. All you mean is to finish us — did you not send to call us? Were not your own messengers the ones who came for us? We are unfortunate, they said; we will go back again. And this was exactly what the boys wanted of them, that they should die there at the game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather those of Xibalba were again defeated by the young men.

Let us play ball, then, with your ball, they were told, and the young men said: very well. And they threw down their own ball, and so the game came to its end for that time. Then those of Xibalba said: what shall we do to overcome them? And they said to the young men: bring us, this coming night, four gourds of flowers — that was the wager they set upon the game. Very well, said the young men. And what flowers? the young men asked those of Xibalba. We want, they said, one gourd of red flowers, one of white, one of yellow, and one of the great flowers, all four gourds full. Very well, said the young men — and it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so.

And then they were sent down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike, all sharp, and the knives were many. This was the second trial of Xibalba, and it was meant that they be cut to pieces by the knives, and quickly, before they could think how to save themselves. But they did not die there; instead they spoke to the flint knives and told them: yours shall be the flesh of every animal, and with this the knives did not stir any more, but stayed still, all of them. And their hearts were glad, those of Xibalba, thinking the two boys already defeated. A good thing we have done, they said in their hearts; where now will they go to get flowers? This very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you, they said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Very well, said the young men, tonight we will play again, they said, when the wager was made.

Then, inside the house of knives, they called to all the ants: come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords. Very well, said the ants, and they all went to bring the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. But those of Xibalba had already warned the one who kept watch over their flowers: let no flowers be carried off, for we have already beaten the two boys, and there is nowhere they can get flowers from — watch all night. Very well, said the guards. But the guards felt nothing; in vain they cried out among the branches of the trees of the garden. And from there came their manner of singing: the one said, xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec, calling it out; the other said, puhuyu, puhuyu — and so the two guards of the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu. And they did not feel the ants carrying off the flowers they guarded, but went turning and shifting among the flowers upon the branches, and with their jaws lifted up those that lay beneath the branches; and the guards kept crying out, and did not feel their own jaws being eaten, nor their wings, nor their tails, and so with their jaws the ants carried off the flowers they gathered, and very quickly they filled the four gourds with flowers, brimming full when it dawned.

Then the messengers, the runners, came, saying: let them come, says the lord, bring here what you have won. Very well, said the young men, and they went carrying the flowers, four gourds full, and they came before the face of the lord, and the lords took the flowers, very soft still, and in this way those of Xibalba were defeated. For it was only the ants that the young men had sent, and in one night the ants had cut the flowers and set them in the gourds, and so all those of Xibalba were terrified, their faces gone pale over the flowers, and they called at once for those who guarded the flowers and said to them: how have you let our flowers be stolen, that we see here? We did not feel it, lord, they said, and see how our own tails are — and their mouths were slit open in payment for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their works against them. And from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion, and so they are found still.

And then they went to play ball once more, and when the game was ended they agreed between themselves, and the two sides gave word to each other that in the morning they would play again. Very well, said the young men, when they left off the game.

I don't know what has bitten me. It bit the next, and he cried, Ay, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you? said the fifth. Ay, ay, said Xiquiripat. And Vucub Came asked him, who has bitten you? And it bit the sixth, and he cried, Ay — what is it, Cuchumaquic, who has bitten you? it was asked. And when it bit the seventh, who cried Ay, what has bitten you, Ahalpuh? said Cuchumaquic. And when it bit the eighth, who cried Ay, Ahalpuh said to him: what is it, Ahalcana, who has bitten you? And when it bit the ninth, seated there, who cried Ay, Ahalcana said to him: Chamiabac, what has bitten you? And when it bit the tenth, who cried Ay, Chamiabac said to him: Chamiaholom, what has bitten you? And biting the eleventh, who cried Ay, it was said to him: what has bitten you? And it bit the twelfth, who cried Ay, and it was said again: what has bitten you, Patan? And biting the thirteenth, who cried Ay, it was said again: what has bitten you, Quicxic? said Patan. And biting the fourteenth, it was said to him, Quicre — what has bitten you? And one, seated on a bench, was named Holoman. And thus all of them spoke their own names, and each declared himself, saying his name — every one of them, when they were bitten by a hair from the face of Hunahpu; and it was not truly a gnat that went and bit them all, and went to hear the names of them all, on behalf of Hunahpu.

Then, when they arrived where the lords of Xibalba were, they were told: go and greet that lord who is seated there. But he was not truly a lord — he was only a carved dummy, dressed up to deceive them. So they said: that is only a dummy. And greeting the rest, they said: Lord Hun Came, Lord Vucub Came, Lord Xiquiripat, Lord Cuchumaquic, Lord Ahalpuh, Lord Ahalcana, Lord Chamiabac, Lord Chamiaholom, Lord Quicxic, Lord Patan, Lord Quicre, Lord Quicxic Chuchah. This they said when they arrived before them all; they spoke the name of every one of them, and not one name was left out, missed, or forgotten. And this was what those of Xibalba had laughed about — that their names would not be known, that the boys would not find them out.

Come, they were told, and they wished to seat them on the bench of honor, but the boys would not sit there: this is not our seat, they said, for it is only a heated stone. They were not defeated by it. Very well, they were told, go then into the house — and they went into a black house, and there too they were not defeated; this was the first trial of Xibalba. They thought to begin their triumph over the boys there. They gave them a torch and, for each of them, a cigar from the messengers of Hun Came, and said: here is your torch and your cigars; the lords say you must return them at dawn, still burning, not used up. Very well, they said. But they did not light the torch; in its place they set a scarlet feather from a macaw's tail, so that to the watching wardens it seemed to burn all night; and in the cigars they set fireflies, so that these too seemed lit. And so the wardens believed all night that the boys were already beaten. But the torch was not consumed, and likewise the cigars were not consumed by them, and in the morning both were carried back whole to the lords.

And they said: what is this, from where have these come, who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for this that they do is not good; strange are their faces and strange their ways. So they said among themselves. And then all the lords sent to summon them: come, let us play ball, young men. And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them: from where have you come? Tell it, young men. But they said, we do not know from where we come, and they did not tell it. Very well, said those of Xibalba, let us go play ball, young men. Where shall we throw down this our ball? said those of Xibalba. By no means shall that one of yours be thrown down, said the young men. And those of Xibalba said, by no means, not that one — only ours. Very well, said the young men.

And then a rounded thing was set before them, dressed up. Let this be it — a worm, called chil, said those of Xibalba. Not so, said the boys; it is not that, but the head of a puma, made bare, its skull, got up to pass for the ball. This is not, said the boys. Very well, said Hunahpu, and threw down the ball of those of Xibalba; and when it came off the bat, a white flint dagger showed itself out from the middle of it, glinting as it went bounding over the floor of the ballcourt. What is this? said the boys. All you mean is to finish us — did you not send to call us? Were not your own messengers the ones who came for us? We are unfortunate, they said; we will go back again. And this was exactly what the boys wanted of them, that they should die there at the game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather those of Xibalba were again defeated by the young men.

Let us play ball, then, with your ball, they were told, and the young men said: very well. And they threw down their own ball, and so the game came to its end for that time. Then those of Xibalba said: what shall we do to overcome them? And they said to the young men: bring us, this coming night, four gourds of flowers — that was the wager they set upon the game. Very well, said the young men. And what flowers? the young men asked those of Xibalba. We want, they said, one gourd of red flowers, one of white, one of yellow, and one of the great flowers, all four gourds full. Very well, said the young men — and it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so.

And then they were sent down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike, all sharp, and the knives were many. This was the second trial of Xibalba, and it was meant that they be cut to pieces by the knives, and quickly, before they could think how to save themselves. But they did not die there; instead they spoke to the flint knives and told them: yours shall be the flesh of every animal, and with this the knives did not stir any more, but stayed still, all of them. And their hearts were glad, those of Xibalba, thinking the two boys already defeated. A good thing we have done, they said in their hearts; where now will they go to get flowers? This very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you, they said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Very well, said the young men, tonight we will play again, they said, when the wager was made.

Then, inside the house of knives, they called to all the ants: come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords. Very well, said the ants, and they all went to bring the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. But those of Xibalba had already warned the one who kept watch over their flowers: let no flowers be carried off, for we have already beaten the two boys, and there is nowhere they can get flowers from — watch all night. Very well, said the guards. But the guards felt nothing; in vain they cried out among the branches of the trees of the garden. And from there came their manner of singing: the one said, xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec, calling it out; the other said, puhuyu, puhuyu — and so the two guards of the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu. And they did not feel the ants carrying off the flowers they guarded, but went turning and shifting among the flowers upon the branches, and with their jaws lifted up those that lay beneath the branches; and the guards kept crying out, and did not feel their own jaws being eaten, nor their wings, nor their tails, and so with their jaws the ants carried off the flowers they gathered, and very quickly they filled the four gourds with flowers, brimming full when it dawned.

Then the messengers, the runners, came, saying: let them come, says the lord, bring here what you have won. Very well, said the young men, and they went carrying the flowers, four gourds full, and they came before the face of the lord, and the lords took the flowers, very soft still, and in this way those of Xibalba were defeated. For it was only the ants that the young men had sent, and in one night the ants had cut the flowers and set them in the gourds, and so all those of Xibalba were terrified, their faces gone pale over the flowers, and they called at once for those who guarded the flowers and said to them: how have you let our flowers be stolen, that we see here? We did not feel it, lord, they said, and see how our own tails are — and their mouths were slit open in payment for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their works against them. And from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion, and so they are found still.

And then they went to play ball once more, and when the game was ended they agreed between themselves, and the two sides gave word to each other that in the morning they would play again. Very well, said the young men, when they left off the game.
revised.translator_note: Revised to fix four fidelity issues flagged in round-2 review, working from the K'iche' (with the Spanish as an aid). (1) The ball Xibalba proposes is now named as the source names it — "a worm, called chil" (Spanish "este gusanío, que se llama chíl"; K'iche' huchil) — rather than mistakenly reusing "Xan," which is the mosquito/gnat from the earlier road episode, a different creature entirely; "Xan" is now used only where the source itself uses it, in the crossroads scene. (2) The ants' summons is now given as direct speech inside the house of knives ("come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords" / "very well, said the ants"), matching "chai zanic, che que'n zanic, quixpetoc..." and the parallel Spanish "hormigas de navajas, hormigas de el muslo, venid...", instead of only mentioning the ants after the fact. (3) The named bird-guards are restored: Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu, with their cries transliterated ("xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec" / "puhuyu, puhuyu"), the lords' forewarning to watch the flowers all night, and the etiology of their manner of calling ("and from there came their manner of singing... so the two guards... are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu"), matching "de allí vino su modo de cantar" and the naming clause in the K'iche'; the later line about their mouths is kept tied to this same etiological pattern ("and from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion") rather than left as a vague aside. (4) The betting sequence is restored: the four gourds of flowers are now explicitly set as the wager on the game ("that was the wager they set upon the game"), the boys' willing self-defeat is rendered plainly ("it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so"), and Xibalba's gloating is given as direct speech in the knife-house scene ("a good thing we have done... where now will they go to get flowers? this very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you"), matching "Buena cosa hemos hecho decían los de el infierno... ya os hemos ganado." Proper names keep the manuscript's own colonial orthography (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, etc.), which the source itself uses and so is not a translator echo. House and object names remain plain literal renderings — "a black house," "house of knives," "white flint dagger," "head of a puma" — deliberately avoiding Tedlock's "Dark House," Goetz-Morley's "House of Gloom," and Christenson's coined equivalents.
