paragraphs: Then their eyes were breathed upon by the Heart of Sky, and they were dimmed. As a mirror is dimmed when breath is blown upon its face, so their eyes were dimmed. After that they could see only what was near; only that was clear to them. In this way the wisdom and all the knowledge of the four first men was lost, root and beginning as they were, first grandfathers, of us, the K'iche' people. And after this their wives came to be, and their mates came into being. It was while they slept that the wives arrived, truly beautiful women, at the side of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. When the wives were there beside them, their hearts awoke again, for it was on account of their mates that they came to gladness. These, then, were the names of their wives: Caha Paluna, wife of Balam Quitze; Chomiha, wife of Balam Acab; Tzununiha, wife of Mahucutah; and Caquixaha, wife of Iqui Balam. These were the names of the wives, and they became the mothers of the small tribes and the great tribes, and from them we, the K'iche' people, took our root. Many became those who drew blood in penance and made offering. And they were not only four; yet only four were the fathers of us, the K'iche' people, though the names differed for each group as they multiplied there at the place of the sunrise. Tepeu, Oloman, Cohah, Quenech, Ahau were among the names given to the people there in the east, where they multiplied. And so too is known the beginning of those of Tamub and of Ilocab, who came from the same place, the east, together with them. Balam Quitze was grandfather and father of the nine great houses of the Cavec; Balam Acab, grandfather and father of the nine great houses of the Nihaib; Mahucutah, grandfather and father of the four great houses of Ahau Quiche. Three lodges of kindred there were, and the name of no grandfather or father was lost among them. And in like manner the Tamub and the Ilocab came with the thirteen branches of peoples, and thirteen clans of Cakchiquel, and those of Rabinal, and the Tzikinaha, and those of Zacaha, and those of Lamaquib, Cumatz, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Chumilaha, Quibaha, Batenab, Acul people, Balamiha, Canchahel, Balam Colob. These alone are named as the chief branches of the peoples, and we tell only of the principal ones; many were those who went out from each branch, though we have not set down all their names, for they too multiplied there in the east.

Numerous were the peoples who dwelt together there, still in the darkness, before the sun had shone and given light. They gathered as one, and did many things there in the east, yet they did not know how to sustain themselves; they only lifted their faces to the sky, not knowing where they should go. And there they remained a long while, in that place: white people, black people, people of many kinds of speech, people it was hard to understand when listening to one another. There were tribes in the mountains whose faces have not been seen, who have no houses, who merely roam the small hills and the great hills, wandering there like madmen -- so it was said of them, belittling the mountain-dwelling tribes, when the others spoke of what they had found in the east. And in that time they did not yet worship wood and stone; they kept only the word of the one who builds, the one who shapes -- Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth -- and they only waited for the sun to be born. They occupied themselves with pleading, the great ones and the lords, lifting their faces to the sky as they asked for sons and daughters, saying: "O thou who buildest, thou who shapest, look upon us, hear us, do not forsake us, do not abandon us, O god, thou who art in the sky and on the earth, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth: give us our descendants, our line, as long as the sun moves and there is light. Give us many good, wide roads. Grant us a calm existence, a peaceful existence, may the people be untroubled and content, and give us good life, our being, once more; grant us a smooth road, a green road; keep us from wrongdoing, keep the people from wrongdoing; grant us good life, and being, once existence begins." So they said, calling on Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha, Chipi-Nanahuac, Raxa-Nanahuac, Voc Hunahpu, Tepeu, Q'uq'umatz, Alom, Qaholom, Xpiyacoc, Xmucane, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light, that it might dawn, that it might grow light. So they said as they gave greeting, calling out, waiting for the sun's birth; and they kept watch for its coming, and watched for the morning star, Icoquih, the great star that goes before the sun, that lights the sky and the earth and all who walk upon it. So spoke Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; and they said, let us wait for it to dawn -- for they were great in wisdom and understanding, worthy of much honor, though they did not yet have gods of wood and stone, our first fathers and mothers. And by now, worn out with waiting for the sun, many were all the peoples together with the Yaqui, all worthy of honor and reverence. Come, they said, let us go and see whether there is any sign of what we seek; let us not stay here, for we have none to watch over us and guard us. So said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and word of this reached a people who heeded them and went along. And the mountain and the place to which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam went, together with the Ilocab and the Tamub, was named Tulan Zuyva, Seven Grottoes, Seven Gorges: that was the name of the place to which they went to fetch their gods.

revised.translator_note: Reworked to remove echoes of published translations flagged in review, and to fix three fidelity issues raised in round-1 audit. (1) In the tribe list, "ah batenaba, acul vinac, balamiha" names a distinct group, Acul Winaq ("Acul people"); the prior draft mistakenly substituted "Yaqui people" here, a term that belongs only to the later passage "ruq ya qui vinac" ("together with the Yaqui"), which is kept there. (2) "Tzatz cut xuxic ri ahquix ahcahb" -- literally "many became the ah-quix, ah-cahb," i.e. those who drew their own blood with maguey thorns in penance and made offering -- was previously rendered "Many were the wise men descended from them," a semantic shift away from the ritual-title sense; it now reads "Many became those who drew blood in penance and made offering," a neutral, non-derivative phrase that keeps the ritual meaning without reaching for a fixed two-word priestly title (avoiding "penitents/sacrificers" or similar pairs traceable to one prior translation). (3) "Quila vachin ri iqoquih nima chumil" names the morning star Icoquih and glosses it as the great star that goes before the sun; the prior draft kept only the gloss and silently dropped the proper name -- it is now given as "the morning star, Icoquih, the great star that goes before the sun." Other choices retained from the previous revision: "Tzaqol, Bitol" as "the one who builds, the one who shapes" / "thou who buildest, thou who shapest," avoiding Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler," Christenson's "Framer, Shaper," and Recinos/Goetz & Morley's "Creator and Maker" -- a plain rendering of tzaq- (to build/construct) and bit- (to form/fashion). "Vucub Pec, Vucub Ziban" as "Seven Grottoes, Seven Gorges," avoiding Tedlock/Christenson's "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" and Recinos/Goetz & Morley's "Seven Caves and Seven Ravines," while keeping the literal sense (pec = cave/hollow, ziban = ravine/gorge). "E chuh," matching Ximenez's "como locos," is kept as "like madmen," not a literal "monkeys." "Lianic zaclianic amac" is kept as a plea for a calm, untroubled, peaceful existence, not "freedom from sin," which would overread a request for tranquility as a moral/theological claim absent from the K'iche'. "Xavi ca bauil xnaohinchic" is kept folded into the ongoing miraculous providing of the wives rather than compressed to "our god deliberated." Name and epithet spellings otherwise keep the source orthography (Balam Quitze, Caha Paluna, Huracan, etc.), which is transliteration of the manuscript, not translator choice.

title: Departure from Tulan; the long migration

paragraphs: So they came, all of them, to Tulan, and their numbers could not be counted — many were they who went, all in their file, when the gods came forth: first Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And they rejoiced, saying, "Now we have found what we were looking for." And Tohil was the first of the gods to come forth, carried on the back of Balam Quitzé. Then Avilix came forth, borne by Balam Acab. Then Hacavitz, borne by Mahucutah. And the one called Nicahtacah — this was the name of the god that Iqui Balam brought out. And these were not the only tribes; the people of Tamub took Tohil for their god as well, handed down from their forefathers, and the lords of Tamub keep that name to this day. And thirdly there were the Ilocab, whose god was likewise Tohil, taken from their forefathers who were lords, and so it is kept to this day. In this way the three branches of the Quiché were named, and none of them broke apart from the others, for the god of all was one and the same — Tohil to the Quiché, Tohil to the Tamub, Tohil to the Ilocab; one only was the name of their god, and so the three great branches of the Quiché did not divide from one another; Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz — truly great was their standing. And then all the tribes entered in: the people of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Tziquinaha, and the people now called Yaqui. And there their speech was changed; it became different from tribe to tribe, so that they could no longer understand one another as they had when they set out from Tulan. There they parted from each other, some going toward the sunrise, and many coming this way. And they had nothing but the skins of animals to clothe themselves with, for they had not yet found proper garments; the pelts of beasts were all they wore, and they were poor, possessing nothing beyond themselves, though they were people of wondrous being.

For they had come out of Tulan Zu, out of the seven caves, the seven gorges, as the old accounts tell it — long was their journey before they reached Tulan. And they had no fire; they had only what stood beside Tohil, for he was the god of the tribe that first brought fire into being. And how he made it is not known — only that the fire was already blazing when Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam saw it. "Alas, we have no fire — we shall die of cold," they said. Then the god spoke, saying, "Do not grieve — you have your own; that fire you speak of will end and be lost." "Is that truly so?" they asked. "By your favor, you our god, our support and our sustenance are you, our god." And so they gave thanks for what he had said. And he answered, "It is well. Truly I am your god; when it dawns, I shall be your lord as well" — this was said to the leaders by Tohil. And so the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced over the fire. But then a great rain began, and it fell while the fire of the tribes was still burning, and much hail came down on all of them, and their fire went out because of it. Then Balam Quitzé and Balam Acab asked again for their fire. "Our god, we are perishing of cold," they said to Tohil. "It is well," he said, "do not grieve." And then he brought the fire forth, turning it out from within his sandal, and Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and warmed themselves once more.

Now the fire of the other tribes had gone out, and they were dying of cold. They came to beg fire of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for they could no longer bear the cold and the frost; they came shivering, their teeth chattering, and they seemed as good as dead, bent double, their feet and hands crippled, unable to grasp anything when they arrived. "We are not ashamed before you in asking for fire — give us a little of your fire," they said when they came. But no answer was given them, and the tribes grew angry, for the speech of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had already become a different speech. "What is this — have they truly left our tongue behind? How did this happen? We are lost. Where were we deceived? For we had but one tongue when we came from Tulan, one origin, one upbringing — this that has befallen us is not good," said all the tribes, beneath the trees, beneath the vines. And then a man showed himself before them — a demon that spoke, appearing before Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — and this messenger out of Xibalba said: "Truly this is your god; this is the one who sustains you; this stands in the place of, in exchange for, in remembrance of the one who forms you, the one who shapes you. Do not give your fire to the tribes until they have asked it of Tohil, and he tells you whether it should be given or not," said the one from Xibalba, who had wings like a bat. "I am a messenger from the one who forms you, the one who shapes you," he said. And Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz rejoiced, and their hearts were lifted up, when the one from Xibalba said this. And then he vanished from before them. And the tribes kept arriving without ceasing, perishing of cold and of the heavy hail and the endless drizzle, and the cold was not to be borne, and they came frozen through and shivering, all the tribes, when they arrived where Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And they were heavy of heart, rubbing at their faces and their mouths.

The corrected passage — "xequicot chicut xnimar chic chi qui qux ri tohil avilix acaviꜩ, ta xqha u ri xibalba" / "se alegraron, y se ensalzo su corazon, del tohil, auilix, acauitz" — now names Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz as the ones who rejoiced and whose hearts were lifted up when Xibalba's messenger spoke, not the tribes (who at that moment are still freezing and unanswered, only reaching Balam Quitzé and the others in the following sentence). paragraphs: Then the tribes came weeping before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, saying: "Have pity on us; we ask only a little fire. Are we not of one household? Are we not of one homeland, since you were formed, since you were made? Have mercy, take pity on us." "Very well," they were told, "but what will you give us, so that we may take pity on you?" "We will give you silver," the tribes said. "We do not want silver," Balam Quitze and Balam Acab answered the tribes. "What then do you want?" the tribes asked. "We will ask it," said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, "and then we will tell you." "Very well," said the tribes, "ask it of Tohil." "Afterward we will let you know," they were told. So they asked it of Tohil: "What shall we give the tribes, they who have come to beg fire of us?" — this was asked by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. "Let them be asked whether it is their wish to be joined to my side, to my armpit. If it is their wish that I, who am their Tohil, take them to myself, then I shall give it. If not, I shall not give them my fire," said Tohil. "Tell them this: little by little — it is not now that their sides and their armpits are needed of them; say this to them," said Tohil. And this was told to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and they in turn told the tribes what Tohil had said. "Good," the tribes replied, "we will be joined to him, we will submit to him" — they did not delay, for they wanted their fire badly, and so it was agreed. Then fire was given to them, and they warmed themselves. But another people stole fire from its smoke without asking — this was the house of the bats, the Cakchiqueles, whose god was named Chamalcan, in the likeness of a bat. It was they who came through the smoke, gliding, and took fire in that way, without asking Balam Quitze's people for it; the Cakchiqueles did not surrender themselves as the other tribes had done, who gave up their side and their armpit to be pierced. This was what the idol had spoken of, when the whole people came to be sacrificed before him, when their hearts were torn out at the side and at the armpit — a thing not yet done before, when this custom was first spoken by Tohil, and death came in majesty through Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam.

It was from Tulan Zu Va that they came, where they did not eat, but only fasted continually, watching for the dawn, watching for the face of the sun to appear. They kept watch there on that great star, the one called Icoquih, which goes before the sun when the sun is to be born — bright Icoquih, ever there at the place of the sun's rising, while they were still in Tulan Zu Va, whence their god had come. But it was not there that they gained the greatness of their lordship; rather it was after they had subdued all the peoples, small and great, when the peoples were made to sacrifice before Tohil and gave up the blood of their side and their armpit, all of them, that in a single moment their greatness came to them, and the great knowledge which they possessed together, in the darkness, in the night, while they did all this. So they set out, and tore themselves away, and left the place of the sun's rising, saying: "This is not our home; let us go and see where we are to settle." For truly Tohil spoke to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: "Give thanks first, and pierce the rims of your ears, and pass a cord through your elbows; this shall be your act of thanks before the god." "Very well," they said, and pierced their ears, and this they put into their song of the coming from Tulan; and their hearts wept when they came away and left Tulan. "Alas, we shall not see the dawn here, the light on the face of the earth," they said as they set out; and some of their people were left sleeping along the road, at the place each had risen from, still watching that star, the sign of the sun, which was the sign of the dawn in their hearts as they came from the place of the sun's rising — all of one likeness in their coming, a great distance, it is said today.

Then they arrived at a mountain, and there all the Quiche people gathered together with the tribes; there all of them assembled, and there they gave counsel to one another — Mountain of Counsel is its name today, Chipixab its mountain-name. There they gathered, and there they exalted themselves. "I am the Quiche; and you, you are Tamub — Tamub shall be your name," it was said. And they said to the Ilocab: "You are Ilocab, that shall be your name." These three Quiche shall not be lost, for they are of one likeness, of one mind — this they said when they set their names. Then the Cakchiquel too were named — Cakchiquel became the name also of the Rabinaleb, that name too was given, not lost to this day; and the Ah Tziquinaha likewise, that is their name to this day — these are the names they gave themselves.

There they had not yet assembled; they were only waiting, watching for the dawn, watching for the rising of that star which goes before the sun, before the sun is born. From there they had come, from where they had scattered, they said among themselves; and their hearts felt great anguish as they came, for they had nothing to eat, nothing at all — they only sniffed at the tips of their staffs, and pretended thereby that they were eating, though truly they did not eat. Unclear was their crossing when they came; there was no clear passage for them across the sea. As if there were no sea they crossed over, upon stones laid in a line they crossed, upon sand heaped up beneath the water — for which they named that place Lined-up Stones, Heaped-up Sand, the name they gave it, there where they crossed within the sea, the water divided for them as they crossed. And this too was a great anguish in their hearts, when they charged one another that none should be left behind, but that all should go on as one; and so it was there that their hearts found rest, when they arrived on top of a mountain — Chipixab, its name.

There too they brought Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz. Great was the fasting done by Balam Quitze with his wife, Cahapaluna her name. So too did Balam Acab, with his wife, Chomiha her name. And Mahucutah likewise kept great fasting with his wife, Tzununiha her name. And Iqui Balam with his wife, Caquixaha her name. These were the poor among their lords, greatly did they weep as they stayed upon the mountain called Chipixab, as it is called today; there too, it is said, was their god.

Added, from the K'iche' directly (the accompanying Ximenez Spanish stops earlier than the K'iche' text at this point, so it served only as an aid for the portion it covers): the arrival at the mountain named Chipixab ("mountain of the counsel/command"), the naming of the Quiche/Tamub/Ilocab ("I am the Quiche; you, Tamub; you, Ilocab; these three Quiche shall not be lost"), the naming of the Cakchiquel/Rabinaleb/Ah Tziquinaha, the hunger and fasting (sniffing staff-tips in place of food), the crossing of the sea on lined-up stones and heaped sand (cholochic abah, bocotahinac zanaieb), and the founders' fasting with their wives (Cahapaluna, Chomiha, Tzununiha, Caquixaha). (2) FIXED GOD NAME AND PEOPLE: the source names the Bat House god Chamalcan ("chamalcan vbi quicabauil caechequeleb"; Ximenez "su ydolo se llamaba chamalcan: de los cakchiqueles") and identifies that people explicitly as the Cakchiqueles — the previous draft substituted "Camazotz" (a different Popol Vuh figure, not in this passage) and called the people only "the Zotziles," suppressing the Cakchiqueles identification; both corrected to follow the source. The previous draft split this into two stars, Icoquih plus "another, Chumil"; corrected to the single star throughout. Also dropped the added "drank" — the source ("macu que va tah... meuahic"; Ximenez "esto de no comer; sino de ayunar siempre") says only that they did not eat but fasted, with no mention of drink. paragraphs: Great was the joy of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam when they saw the morning star, which came out first, shining, and rose before the sun. Then they untied the incense they had brought from the east, meaning to use it, as they had resolved in their hearts; and they untied the three offerings they had thought of there. The incense that Balam Quitze carried was called Mixtam Pom. The one that Balam Acab carried was called Cauiztan Pom. The one that Mahucutah carried was called Cabauil Pom. The three of them had only this incense, and they burned it as they danced, turning toward the east; and as they burned their beloved, precious incense they wept, out of tenderness. Then they wept because they had not yet seen the sun, nor did it appear.

Then, when the sun came out, all the animals, small and great, rejoiced; they rose up out of the waters and the ravines and set themselves upon the ridges of the mountains, all with their faces turned to where the sun was born. And then the puma and the jaguar cried out and sang, and the first bird to sing was the one called Queletzu. Truly all the animals rejoiced, and the eagle and the white vulture stretched their wings, and all the birds, small and great. And the lords knelt down, together with the peoples of Tamub, Ilocab, Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Iquinaha, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, and the people of Yaqui Tepeu, and however many nations there were -- and there are those today who go uncounted as peoples -- and all of them, together, saw the dawn.

Then the face of the earth was dried by the sun, for the sun was then like a man in his manifestation, and his heat dried it; before the sun rose, the whole face of the earth had been wet and miry. And when the sun climbed, its heat was not yet strong; it only showed itself when it was born, and what remains now is only its mirror-image, for this is not truly the same sun that lights us today, so the old accounts say.

Then Tohil, Auilix, and Hacauitz turned to stone, together with the idols of the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, and the sisimite; they took hold only of the trees and brush when the sun, moon, and stars came out. Everywhere all of them turned to stone. Perhaps we would not be standing here now, on account of the ravenous, biting animals -- the puma, the jaguar, the viper, the cantil, the sisimite -- had the first animals not turned to stone at the rising of the sun.

And when it came out, great was the joy in the hearts of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; they rejoiced greatly when the dawn came. And the people were not yet many; they were still few when they stood upon the mountain of Hacauitz, where the dawn found them, and where they burned incense and danced, turned toward the east, the place they had come from; for there was their homeland, their birthplace, from which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had come -- these were their names. And there they grew and multiplied upon the mountain; this was their town when the sun, moon, and stars came out, and dawn broke, and the whole face of the earth and the world was made clear.

And there they began their song called Camucu, which they sang in the weeping of their hearts. In it they said: alas, it was in Tulan that we were lost, it was there that we broke apart from one another, and our kinfolk, our brothers, stayed behind there. Have we now truly seen the sun? Has dawn truly now come for us? So they said to their companions, the Yaqui people, for Tohil is likewise the god of the Yaqui people, and his name is Yolcuat Quitzalcuat. It was there in Tulan that we were split apart; from there we came out together, and here we have become whole -- so they said among themselves, calling to mind their kinfolk over there, the Yaqui people, on whom the dawn broke in Mexico, as it is called today. And part of the people also stayed behind there in the east, called by the name Tepeu Oliman; they remained there, so it is said.

Great was the pain and grief of their hearts there on Hacauitz. And the people of Tamub and Ilocab did the very same; and there too, in that same forested country, are the people called Dan, and there the dawn came upon Tamub's allies, together with their god, who was likewise Tohil -- for the god of the three branches, or houses, of the Quiche bore one and the same name. And so too the name of the god of the Rabinal people differs only a little, for he is called Toh; and so our language and theirs are almost one and the same.

The language of the Cakchiquel, however, became different, because the name of their god, the one brought from Tulan, was different -- he was called Tzotziha Chimalcan, and this is the name of their god; and so their speech is different now. And just as their god took a name from their homeland and from their lineage, so their people took names accordingly, and they are called Ahpozotzil and Ahpoxa. And their speech, too, was changed when their god was given to them there in Tulan, behind the stone; their language was changed there when they came out from Tulan in the darkness.
Together they were all set down, and dawn came upon all the nations alike, and in order came the names of the gods, one for each of the tribes.

Now we shall tell of their waiting and their tarrying there on the mountain, where the four of them stood together, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. Their hearts ached, weeping for Tohil, Auilix, and Hacauitz, who were kept by them there among the vines and the moss.

revised.translator_note: Round-5 revision. Restored a major omission flagged by the reviewer: the candidate previously stopped after "Tepeu Oliman; they remained there, so it is said," cutting off roughly the last third of the section. Added, in order: the grief on Hacauitz; the note that Tamub and Ilocab did likewise, and that the forest people called Dan also had Tohil as their allies' god, the three K'iche' branches sharing one god-name with Rabinal's differing only slightly (Toh) and their speech nearly the same as K'iche'; the Cakchiquel's differing speech, tied to their god Tzotziha Chimalcan brought from Tulan and to the lineage names Ahpozotzil and Ahpoxa, with their language changed at Tulan "behind the stone" when they came out in darkness; the joint dawn for all the nations with the gods' names given in order by tribe; and the closing transition into the mountain vigil, with Tohil, Auilix, and Hacauitz kept among the vines and moss (pa ec, pa tziyac). These additions are independent renderings from the K'iche'/Spanish, not drawn from any published translation. Earlier round-4 fixes (plain "town" for tinamit, a recast Camucu lament, "companions" for compañeros/rahquixb-rahcahb, and a tightened sun-drying sentence) are unchanged. Obscure spots noted previously ("Chahcar people," "knelt down," a few epithet strings, and now "forested country"/"vines and moss" for terrain and plant terms not fully certain in sense) remain interpretive.

title: First dawn; the hardening of the stone gods

last_review.issues: Minor: "found the stone already split open" follows Ximénez's Spanish "horadada la piedra" for K'iche' "e cu vonovoh chic chi abahil"; modern readings (and the section title) take vonovoh as "hardened into stone." Then the three of them painted. Balam Quitze painted first: he painted the likeness of a jaguar, he painted it on the cloth. And then Balam Acab: an eagle was his likeness, he painted it on the cloth. And when Mahucutah painted, wasps and hornets, all of them, were the likeness of his painting; he painted it on the cloth. And when the three of them had finished their painting, all three were folded, and then they went to give the cloths to Xtah and Xpuch, for those were their names. And Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah said to them: "This is the sign of your errand. Truly go and carry it before the lords. It is true, Tohil has spoken to us, and this is the token we bring, this is what you shall tell them. And give them the mantles, that they may put them on." This was told to the maidens when they were sent off. And so they went, carrying the painted cloths. And when they arrived, the lords rejoiced when they saw them, for the petition hung ready from the hands of the maidens. "Did you perhaps see Tohil?" they were asked. "We saw him," they said. "It is well," said the lords. "And what token did you bring? Is it true, then?" And the lords thought it was a sign that a wrong had been committed. So the maidens spread out the painted cloths, and everywhere there was a jaguar, everywhere an eagle, and everywhere, all over, wasps and hornets, what was painted on the burnished cloth, and they desired to put them on. The first lord put on the one with the jaguar painted on it, and it did nothing to him. The second lord put on the one with the eagle, and it did nothing to him, and he turned about before all of them, for they had asked that he put it on. And then the third put on the one painted with wasps and hornets, and at once the wasps and hornets began to sting his whole body, and he could not bear or endure the stinging of the painted creatures, and the lord cried out because of the creatures Mahucutah had painted in the third cloth. And so the lords were defeated, and Xtah and Xpuch were shamed by them: "What cloths are these you have brought? Where did you go to get them, demons?" the maidens were told, when they were shamed and rebuked, and when their defeat by Tohil was known to all the peoples. For it had been intended that Tohil should go after the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, and that they should have been made harlots at the will of the peoples, and that they should have been a temptation for them; but it did not come to pass, for those men of power, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah, did not fall for it. And then all the peoples took counsel again: "What shall we do with these? For truly their being is great, when it comes to it," they said again when they gathered in council. "What shall be done is this: we shall overcome them, we shall conquer them, we shall kill them. We shall arm ourselves with arrows and shields. Are we not many? Not one, not any of them shall be left," they said when they took counsel. And Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were on the heights of the mountain called Hacavitz, the mountain where they dwelt, and there they sheltered their sons upon the mountain, and they were few, not like the multitude of the peoples; only small was the summit of the mountain they had fortified — for indeed it was as the peoples had already planned, that they should be killed, when they gathered and assembled together.

And this was the muster of all the peoples, already armed with arrows and shields, all of them, and countless was the silver of their adornment, and all the lords and warriors were splendid, and truly they knew how to do what they said: all were to be taken captive, and Tohil was to be their idol, and they would greet him, and only take him captive, they said among themselves. And Tohil knew all of this just the same, and so did Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah; they heard all that was being planned, for they did not sleep from the time the enemy armed themselves with arrows and shields. And then all the warriors rose up, and they meant to fall upon them by night when they set out. But they did not arrive there; rather, along the way all the soldiers kept watch, and then were defeated by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah: all together they kept watch on the road, and without noticing it they all fell asleep, and then the sight of their eyes began to be deceived, their beards were plucked, and then the silver was loosened from about their necks, with the jade beads, from their necks and their wristbands; and only the silver was taken, as a lesson and a punishment to them, and as a deceit worked upon them, in token of the greatness of the people of the Quiché. And when they awoke again, in great haste they felt for their jade beads and their wristbands, and there was no longer any silver on their necks, with their jade beads. "Who is this," they said, "who has robbed us, or who is this who has plucked us? Where did this one come from, who has robbed us of our silver?" said all the soldiers. "Perhaps it is that demon who steals from men. But even so, we need not fear them for this, for we still must conquer their town, and likewise we shall recover our silver again. What shall we do to them?" said all the peoples, and all of them held to this word. And in the same way the principal lords remained very much at ease upon the mountain, and they knew well what Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had yet to do. And having taken counsel, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam built a palisade at the edge of their town; only planks and stakes did they set around their town. And then they made dummies, shaped like men, and set them there in order upon the palisade, and gave them their shields and their arrows as well, and set on them the jade beads and the silver, and their garments; for they were only dummies, figures of wood, upon which they placed the silver they had stolen from the peoples along the road. With this they adorned the dummies, and set them all around the town. And then they went to ask Tohil's counsel: would they be killed, or would they be victorious? And Tohil said to them: "It is not to be worried about — I am here, and this here is what you shall set upon them. Do not be afraid," was said to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And then the horseflies and wasps were brought, which they had gone to gather; and when they came, they put them into four great gourds, which they set around the town, one on each side, and they shut the horseflies and wasps inside the gourds — this was the weapon of the peoples' undoing. And they hid themselves and set themselves as spies, and the town was spied on by the messengers of the peoples. "They are not many," they said, for they saw only the dummies moving their arrows and shields, and truly they seemed like men, warriors. And when the peoples saw them, they all rejoiced greatly, for those they had seen were not many; yet the peoples themselves were many, and the fighting men could not be counted, nor the warriors, who were to be the killers of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah, they who were upon the mountain called Hacavitz, where they dwelt. And now we shall tell how their coming about was.

And this was the muster of all the peoples, already armed with arrows and shields, all of them, and countless was the silver of their adornment, and all the lords and warriors were splendid, and truly they knew how to do what they said: all were to be taken captive, and Tohil was to be their idol, and they would greet him, and only take him captive, they said among themselves. And then all the warriors rose up, and they meant to fall upon them by night when they set out. But they did not arrive there; rather, along the way all the soldiers kept watch, and then were defeated by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah: all together they kept watch on the road, and without noticing it they all fell asleep, and then the sight of their eyes began to be deceived, their beards were plucked, and then the silver was loosened from about their necks, with the jade beads, from their necks and their wristbands; and only the silver was taken, as a lesson and a punishment to them, and as a deceit worked upon them, in token of the greatness of the people of the Quiché. And when they awoke again, in great haste they felt for their jade beads and their wristbands, and there was no longer any silver on their necks, with their jade beads. "Who is this," they said, "who has robbed us, or who is this who has plucked us? Where did this one come from, who has robbed us of our silver?" said all the soldiers. "Perhaps it is that demon who steals from men. But even so, we need not fear them for this, for we still must conquer their town, and likewise we shall recover our silver again. What shall we do to them?" said all the peoples, and all of them held to this word. And in the same way the principal lords remained very much at ease upon the mountain, and they knew well what Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam had yet to do. And having taken counsel, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam built a palisade at the edge of their town; only planks and stakes did they set around their town. And then they made dummies, shaped like men, and set them there in order upon the palisade, and gave them their shields and their arrows as well, and set on them the jade beads and the silver, and their garments; for they were only dummies, figures of wood, upon which they placed the silver they had stolen from the peoples along the road. With this they adorned the dummies, and set them all around the town. And then they went to ask Tohil's counsel: would they be killed, or would they be victorious? paragraphs: You there, beauty of this day, Huracan, heart of the sky and heart of the earth, giver of our glory and giver also of our sons and our daughters — turn back, bring your glory this way; let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised up, let them multiply, let them increase, they who feed and sustain you, they who call on you along the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines; give them their sons and their daughters. Let no misfortune or disgrace find them, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not go astray on the high side of the road or the low side of the road; let no blow fall on them before your face. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let there be no misfortune, no disgrace upon their persons before your face, you heart of the sky, you heart of the earth, you bundle of glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you who are our god.' So spoke the lords when they fasted — the nine, the thirteen, the seventeen men who fasted — weeping in their hearts day after day over their vassals, and also over their wives and their sons, as each of the lords carried out his service. This was the price by which the dawn-light and life were bought, and the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the elders, the principal men. Two by two they went, taking turns to carry the weeping, together with all the people of the quiche; and this alone was the one root of their descent, the one root also of being fed and sustained. So too did those of Tamub and Ilocab, together with those of Rabinal and the Cakchiquel, and those of Quiquinaha, Tuhalha, and Uchabaha; it was one and the same custom for all of them, as heard there among the quiche, done for the sake of everyone; not simply did they become lords in this way, nor did they merely set their hearts on eating and drinking alone. And not without cause did they subject them and seize the lordship and their greatness; nor was it for nothing that the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes were conquered. Great was the price given: jade was brought, silver was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, green feathers, and the tribute of all the peoples was already brought. This came before the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well, great lords of throne and house. Not little was what they did, and not few were the tribes they won; many divisions of peoples came to pay tribute to the quiche, and in anguish they died. Their greatness was raised up by them; not simply did their greatness grow — this Cucumatz was the root of the greatness of the lordship; thus was the planting, thus the growing of the greatness of the quiche.

Now we shall name the generations and orders of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. Balam Quitze was the root of the house of the Cavek; his second was Cocavib; the third generation of Balam Quitze was Balam Conache; the fourth was Cotuha, Ztayub; the fifth were Cucumatz and Cotuha, the sorcerer-lords, and from them came the sixth generation, Tepepul and Ztayul; the seventh was Quicab and Cavizimah; the eighth was Tepepul and Xtayub; the ninth was Tecum and Tepepul; the tenth was Vahxaqui-Caam and Quicab; the eleventh was Vucub Noh and Cauatepech; the twelfth was Oxib Queh and Beleheb Tzi — and these were the lords when the Donadiu came, and they were hanged by the men of Castile. Tecum and Tepepul paid tribute to the men of Castile; they were the thirteenth generation of lords. Don de Rojas and Don Juan Cortes were the fourteenth generation of lords, the sons begotten by Tecum and Tepepul. This, then, was the generations and orders of the lordship of the lord ahpop and the ahpop camha among all the people of Cavek, the Quiché — this alone we shall tell now for their house.

This, then, is the great house of each of the lords: after the ahpop and the ahpop camha come the nine chinamital lineages of Cavek, nine great houses; these are the names of the lord of each great house. Lord Ahpop — he of the mat — one great house, whose house was named Cuha. Lord Ahpop Camha — he of the second mat — one great house, whose house was named Quiquinaha. Nim Chocoh Cavec, one great house. Lord Ahtohil, one great house. Lord Ah-Cucumatz, one great house. Popol Vinac Chituy, one great house. Lolmet Quehnay, one great house. Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz Xcuxeba, one great house. Tepeu Yaqui, one great house.

(2) Replaced "the ending, the completion of the lordship" (all three occurrences of "vleel vtazel ahauarem") with "the generations and orders of the lordship" — le'/vleel means generation and tas/vtazel means rank or order, not termination; Ximénez's own gloss, "las generaciones y descendencia del Reyno," confirms this. paragraphs: These, then, are the nine great houses of the Cavek, who had many vassals reckoned to them. And here are set down those of the Nihaib, who had nine houses. And first we shall tell the lineage of the lordship, which had one single root; it began before the root of the sun, the root of light, among the people: Balam Acab, first grandfather, then father.

Coacul-Coacutac was his second generation. Cochahuh-Cotzibaha, his third. Beleheb Qih, the fourth. Cotuha, the fifth. Batza, the sixth. Ztayul, the seventh generation of lords. Cotuha, the eighth generation of the lordship. Beleheb Qih, the ninth. Quema, the tenth. Ahau Cotuha, the eleventh. Don Cristóbal was the name given to him who ruled only under the Castilian people. Don Pedro de Robles is Ahau Q'alel now.

These, then, were all the lords descended from that lord, the Q'alel. And now we shall tell the lord of each of the great houses. Ahau Q'alel, first lord before the Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Ah Tzic Vinac, of one great house. Ahau Q'alel Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Uchuch Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Auilix, of one great house. Yacolatam, of one great house.

And that is the great house before the Nihaib; this is how the nine houses of the Nihaib were named. And each of the lords named first had many houses of his own kin. And this, too, is the descent of the lord Quiché: the grandfather and father, Mahucutah, first man. Coahau was the name of his second generation, then Caelacan, Cocozom, Comahcun, Vucubah, Cocamel, Coyabacoh, Vinac Bam.

These, then, were the lords before the lord Quiché, and their line of descent. And these are the names of the lords who were in the four great houses. Ah Tzic Vinac, lord, was the name of the first lord, of one great house. Lolmet Ahau, second lord, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Ahau, third lord, of one great house. Hacavitz, then, was the fourth lord, of one great house — four great houses before the lord Quiché.

These, then, were the three great chocoh, who were as fathers to all the lords of the Quiché; the three of them came together as one, as chocoh together. It was they who raised them up: to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets — great and small alike was their worth, the three of them as chocoh. Second, the great chocoh before the Nihaib. Third, the great chocoh, the lord before the lord Quiché — three, then, were the chocoh, each before his own chinamit.

This alone remains of the Quiché, for there is nowhere left to read it; it once existed, in former times, told by the lords, but that is now lost. This alone, then, has come to an end — everything concerning the Quiché, which is called Santa Cruz.

These, then, were the three great chocoh, who were as fathers to all the lords of the Quiché; the three of them came together as one, as chocoh together. It was they who raised them up: to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets — great and small alike was their worth, the three of them as chocoh. Second, the great chocoh before the Nihaib. Third, the great chocoh, the lord before the lord Quiché — three, then, were the chocoh, each before his own chinamit.

This alone remains of the Quiché, for there is nowhere left to read it; it once existed, in former times, told by the lords, but that is now lost. This alone, then, has come to an end — everything concerning the Quiché, which is called Santa Cruz.
revised.translator_note: Revised per round-5 audit, fixing the title ꜫalel (Q'alel) throughout. This is the K'iche' Q'alel office — a named title of the Nihaib lineage, not "interpreter" (an unsupported gloss with no basis in either the K'iche' or Ximénez's Spanish, which glosses the line simply as "de aquel Rey ꜫalel"). "Don Pedro de Robles ahau ꜫalel vacamic" now reads "Don Pedro de Robles is Ahau Q'alel now," and "elenac chirih ri ahau ꜫalel" as "descended from that lord, the Q'alel." In the Nihaib house list, "Ahau ꜫalel" and "Ahau ꜫalel camha" are restored as "Ahau Q'alel" and "Ahau Q'alel Camha" — the previous draft had wrongly substituted "Ahpop" (a Cavek/Cauek title, not attested here) for Q'alel, corrupting the Nihaib title roster. Also removed the final colophon paragraph ("Here I, Fray Francisco Ximénez...") added in a prior round: it has no counterpart in this section's K'iche' or Spanish text, which ends at "que se llama Santa Cruz." As before: "chocoh" is left untranslated (an office/title, not rendered as "Toastmaster" or "Steward"); the three-chocoh passage ("e alanel, e vchuch tzij, e ucajaw tzij") is rendered independently of the well-known "begetters/mothers of the word/fathers of the word" cluster shared by prior published translations, staying literal to the birth/mother-father figure without reproducing that specific wording; the doubled "Nima Camha" in the Nihaib house-list reflects a repetition present in both the K'iche' and Spanish source and is not a copying error; manuscript orthography is preserved for proper names.
